result:
**Read it if you're building a SKILL.md linter or rubric; skip it if you want evidence that these problems matter.**

The paper's real deliverable is a 26-item smell catalog (inverted community best practices) plus a 13/44-component taxonomy for SKILL.md files, validated across 238 marketplace skills.

What's directly reusable:
- The smell list splits cleanly into 5 static checks (word/char caps on body/name/description, backslash paths, XML in frontmatter) and 21 LLM-judge checks. That split is the architecture for any detector you'd write.
- Their judge prompt framing: per-smell definition + one positive + one negative example + binary yes/no, thinking mode on. Ran on a quantized Qwen3.6-27B, hit weighted F1 0.78 (precision 0.79, recall 0.78) against 53 hand-labeled files.
- The description rule — [what it does] + [when to use] + [keywords] — works as a standalone trigger-quality check.

Headline findings: >99% of skills have at least one smell, 10.5 on average, one clean file out of 238. Rationalization Loophole (nothing discourages skipping required steps) hits 94%. Smells rarely get fixed once introduced. Only 7 of 13 component types have any community guidance at all.

The reason to be skeptical: the "best practices" are folklore scraped from 29 web pages and settled by majority vote, never causally validated. The paper shows smells are common, not that they hurt agent performance. The 99% number partly reflects that a rubric built from folklore flags nearly everything. Sample is popular public marketplace skills, so it may not transfer to internal ones. Detector numbers rest on 53 files and one 4-bit model.

Skim path: the 26-smell list and the static/judge split are the whole payload. The evolution analysis (1,295 commits) and component prevalence table add little unless you need the structural vocabulary.
